summary: Updates RFC 7030 (Enrollment over Secure Transport) to resolve errata that caused interoperability problems. It deprecates the use of Content-Transfer-Encoding headers for EST endpoints and fixes syntax errors in the ASN.1 definitions used by the protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of fixes to the instructions for how devices ask for security certificates, so that different makers' products stop misunderstanding each other.

subtitle: Fixes to the enrollment protocol for securing devices with certificates.

tldr.problem: RFC 7030 (Enrollment over Secure Transport) had errors in its specifications that caused interoperability problems when implementers extended it, and it incorrectly referenced content-transfer-encoding headers that HTTP standards deprecate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8951 updates RFC 7030 with clarifications: it deprecates the Content-Transfer-Encoding header, fixes ASN.1 syntax errors, clarifies how error messages should be formatted, and specifies that base64 encoding should be used regardless of any transfer-encoding headers.
tldr.outcome: Devices from different manufacturers can now reliably enroll for security certificates without misunderstanding each other's messages, improving interoperability in enterprise and IoT deployments.

today: RFC 8951 is an Internet Standard that updates RFC 7030. Both specifications are actively used in enterprise certificate enrollment systems, including government, utility, and financial deployments. RFC 8951 reflects and clarifies the actual practices of deployed implementations.

sections.title: EST and the Problem It Solves
sections.content:
Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST), defined in RFC 7030, is a protocol that allows devices to request security certificates from a certificate authority over HTTPS. It defines HTTP endpoints where devices can enroll, re-enroll, check for certificate attributes, and request server-generated keys. EST is now widely deployed in enterprise networks, utilities, government systems, and the Internet of Things.

However, RFC 7030 had several issues: it incorrectly specified the use of Content-Transfer-Encoding headers (which HTTP standards deprecated), it contained syntax errors in its ASN.1 module, and it was unclear about error message formats. These errors caused confusion and interoperability problems, especially when implementers extended the protocol (for example, in the BRSKI bootstrapping specification).
sections.plainLanguage: EST is how devices ask a certificate authority for security certificates. The original instructions had mistakes that made different devices confused about what the other was saying.

sections.title: Why These Clarifications Matter
sections.content:
EST is specified using MIME headers rather than pure HTTP, following older conventions. RFC 2616 and later versions of the HTTP specification explicitly deprecated Content-Transfer-Encoding. Despite this, RFC 7030 required the use of this header in multiple endpoints.

Real-world testing showed that many implementations did not actually send the Content-Transfer-Encoding header, and many others ignored it when present. Because implementations were already diverging from the specification, deprecating the header rather than trying to enforce it was the sensible approach.

This document resolves four errata (4384, 5107, 5108, and 5904) that had been reported against RFC 7030. The fixes address content-transfer-encoding handling, ASN.1 syntax, and error message clarity. These changes maintain backward compatibility with existing implementations while clarifying correct behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The original instructions said to use an old MIME feature that HTTP doesn't actually like. Most devices ignored this anyway. This fix makes the instructions match what implementations actually do.

sections.title: Content-Transfer-Encoding Deprecation
sections.content:
RFC 8951 updates multiple EST endpoints to remove references to Content-Transfer-Encoding and clarify the encoding used. The key change is that all EST endpoints now MUST use base64 encoding (as specified in RFC 4648) for certificate data, and this MUST be used regardless of any Content-Transfer-Encoding header value.

The specification now states: when an endpoint requires base64 encoding, the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) are used to encode the certificate data, and then base64 is applied to the result. Implementations MUST ignore any Content-Transfer-Encoding header they receive and always decode base64-encoded payloads.

The affected endpoints include: /cacerts (CA certificates response), /fullcmc (Full PKI request/response), /simpleenroll and /simplereenroll (simple enrollment), /serverkeygen (server-side key generation), and /csrattrs (CSR attributes response). All of these now consistently use base64 encoding without reference to transfer-encoding headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of using a confusing MIME feature, all messages now use base64 encoding. Devices should ignore any old MIME headers and just decode the base64.

sections.title: ASN.1 Module Corrections
sections.content:
RFC 7030 did not include an ASN.1 module, but the document body contained ASN.1 definitions scattered throughout. RFC 8909 creates a new, corrected ASN.1 module (called PKIXEST-2019) by extracting and correcting these definitions.

The module fixes syntax errors that were present in the original document. A key part of this module is the definition of CsrAttrs, which specifies how Certificate Signing Request (CSR) attributes are formatted. These attributes tell a client what certificate parameters the server expects (for example, which cryptographic curves to use, which signature algorithms, or what additional information to include in the certificate request).

IANA has registered the OID for the new ASN.1 module (id-mod-est-2019, 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.0.98) and also updated the reference for the Asymmetric Decryption Key Identifier attribute to include this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The original document had the ASN.1 definitions scattered and had some mistakes. This fixes them and puts them in one place.

sections.title: Error Message Clarifications
sections.content:
One source of confusion in RFC 7030 was the handling of error messages. When an enrollment request fails, the server returns an error response. RFC 7030 stated that if no content-type was set, the response should be a plaintext human-readable error message, but it was unclear whether the server could use a content-type header with such messages.

RFC 8951 clarifies that servers MAY use the "text/plain" content-type for human-readable error messages. This makes it explicit that an error message can carry both a content-type header and plaintext text, which helps clients properly identify error responses and prevents misinterpretation of error messages as valid data.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the server sends a human-readable error message. This fix clarifies that it's okay to label it as plain text, so clients know it's an error.

sections.title: White Space in Base64
sections.content:
Base64 encoding in HTTP (RFC 2616) does not allow line breaks (CRLF), but the MIME version (RFC 2045) does permit them. This specification clarifies that despite the HTTP standard, receivers SHOULD tolerate white space characters including CR (carriage return), LF (line feed), spaces, and tabs when decoding base64.

This tolerance helps with interoperability: some implementations wrap base64 data across multiple lines with CRLF characters for readability or compatibility with legacy systems. Making receivers lenient toward such whitespace prevents unnecessary interoperability failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Base64 text can sometimes have line breaks added for readability. Devices should accept this and just ignore the extra spaces and line breaks.
